No — not without qualification. The 'main effect of condition' in a treatment-coded model with an interaction is not the average effect of condition. It is a simple effect.

What the coefficient actually represents

With treatment coding (the R default, where one level is coded 0 and the other 1), the 'main effect' of factor A in a model with an A × B interaction is the effect of A when B is at its reference level — not the average effect of A across levels of B. Concretely: if your model is y ~ condition * time + (...) with both factors treatment-coded, the condition coefficient estimates the condition difference only at the reference level of time. It is a simple effect, not a marginal (average) effect.

This is a well-known interpretive trap documented by Schad, Vasishth, Hohenstein & Kliegl (2020, Journal of Memory and Language): treatment-coded 'main effects' in interaction models are simple effects under a different name. The magnitude — and even the direction — of that coefficient will change if you choose a different reference level for the other factor, even though the model predictions and the interaction term are unchanged.

Two ways to fix this

Option 1 — Recode the factors before fitting. Switch both factors to sum coding (−1/+1) or contrast coding (−0.5/+0.5). With this coding, the 'main effect' of condition is the effect of condition averaged across levels of the other factor — exactly what you probably meant to report.

```r
contrasts(d$condition) <- matrix(c(-0.5, 0.5), dimnames = list(NULL, "cond"))
contrasts(d$time)      <- matrix(c(-0.5, 0.5), dimnames = list(NULL, "time"))

fit <- lmer(y ~ condition * time + (1 + condition * time | subject), data = d)
# Now 'condition' coefficient = average effect of condition across time levels
```

Option 2 — Keep the current model, use post-estimation to marginalize. Use emmeans or marginaleffects to compute the condition effect averaged over levels of the other factor:

```r
library(emmeans)
emm <- emmeans(fit, ~ condition)
contrast(emm, "pairwise")
```

Or:

```r
library(marginaleffects)
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "condition")
```

Bottom line: Do not report the treatment-coded 'main effect of condition' as 'the average effect of condition.' Either refit with sum/contrast coding, or use emmeans/marginaleffects to compute the marginalized average effect.
